title: F8 – Organizational identity, categories and optimal distinctiveness
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 6 „Organizational Identity & Positioning“ mit dem Oura-Ring-Fall und den Präsentationen zu Durand & Kremp (2016) und Zhao et al. (2017)

blocks.text: Markets are not continuous spaces – they are segmented by categories (movie genres, patent classes, industries, academic disciplines). Audiences use categories to answer two questions: what is it, and how good is it?
A fundamental strategic question is “Who are we as an organization?” – formulating identity goes together with formulating purpose and goals.

Is differentiation always best? Porter says competitive strategy is about being different. Research on categories shows that audiences penalize what they cannot classify – organizations must be as different as legitimately possible (optimal distinctiveness).
Complex or credence goods: quality is hard to assess before consumption. Institutions reduce uncertainty about identity and quality:
children: Formal rules: ownership rights, contract enforcement
Informal rules: routines, beliefs, social norms
Market intermediaries: reviews, ratings, rankings, certifications, accreditations, degrees

blocks.text: Organizational identity (Albert & Whetten 1985) rests on three types of attributes:
children: Centrality: attributes that make the organization what it is – without them it would be different
Durability: attributes that reflect the organization's history and endure over time
Distinctiveness: attributes that separate it from similar organizations

blocks.text: Strategic positioning has two axes: horizontal = identity claim (set of features, industries, categories), vertical = status claim (perceived value, quality, ordering into low, middle and high tiers).
Two-stage valuation: first, audiences screen offers that conform to a recognizable category (secure attention through conformity); only then is differentiation used to attract them.
Zuckerman (1999): diversified firms spanning industry categories are less often covered by industry-specialized financial analysts and receive a lower valuation – the illegitimacy discount.

Innovative identities must be identified, recognized, classified and understood to be valued. People say they want creativity but tend to reject novel ideas (Mueller et al. 2012 – bias against creativity).

sections.heading: Category spanning – the Oura Ring case

blocks.text: Oura (Kickstarter 2015): sleep, heart-rate variability and temperature → “Readiness Score”; titanium design; early adopters (biohackers, NBA players); later Gucci edition (> USD 950), subscription (2021), Apple Health integration, AI advisor (2024), Dexcom partnership (2025). 2.5m rings by mid-2024, ~USD 500m revenue.

The market cannot agree on what it is: sleep tracker, fitness device, luxury accessory or medical tool? Each audience applies a different category and expectations – early adopters (data depth), athletes (benchmarked against WHOOP), mainstream consumers (“what does it replace?”), luxury buyers (tech ages, jewellery lasts), clinicians (validated accuracy), retailers (which aisle?), investors (inconsistent peers).
Category spanners combine features of typical members of more than one category. Innovation often happens at the periphery, by combining elements from several domains.

Ambiguity paradox – liability: confusion at the point of sale, no stable price anchor, discount from analysts and investors lacking peers. Asset: broad appeal and several growth engines, avoids head-on comparison with the Apple Watch or jewellers, flexibility (options to pivot) valued by venture capital.

Five positioning options: A) sleep & recovery specialist (clear identity; smaller market), B) health & clinical device (high barriers; slow, costly, regulatory risk), C) luxury wearable (margins; small volumes, tech obsolescence), D) create the smart-ring category and become its prototype (sets the criteria; a form-based category invites copycats), E) one core, many frames (several growth engines; coordination, identity drift).
Critical lens: individualization of health, datafication of the body and ownership of biometric data, unclear regulation – not all categories can be blurred without risk.

Across domains, category spanners (generalists) receive lower evaluations or performance than specialists (Hsu 2006; Kovács & Hannan 2015 …). Moderators that soften the penalty: audience goals, tastes and expertise; the actor's status or reputation; the novelty of the category.
Pros and cons of spanning (“jack of all trades, master of none?”):
children: Demand side +: perception of resources to handle complex issues, diluted risk
Demand side −: inattention (atypical identities ignored), confusion and cognitive burden, perceived lack of commitment or inauthenticity
Supply side +: economies of scope (synergies), market power, risk dilution
Supply side −: dilution of resources and skills, higher coordination costs

blocks.text: Categories change: BlackBerry had ~20 % of smartphones sold in 2010 and ~0 % in 2025 – the iPhone design became the new prototype; the object changed, the label stayed.

Tension: firms must differentiate to gain competitive advantage (strategic management) and conform to the industry's norms, standards and institutions to gain legitimacy (institutional theory) – “as different as legitimately possible” (Deephouse 1999: strategic balance).

Evidence from music: Askin & Mauskapf (2017, 27,000+ songs): a balanced level of differentiation and conformity (inverted U) predicts the highest chance of a hit. Berger & Packard (2018): lyrical differentiation helps overall, but the effect varies across genres → differentiation must be analysed on N dimensions.
Zhao et al. (2017): optimal distinctiveness is a dynamic process, not a fixed midpoint:
children: Orchestration: integrative (familiar elements, distinctive combination) or compensatory (deviate strongly on one dimension, conform on another)
Stakeholder multiplicity: customers, investors, regulators and employees judge with different criteria (wine in the US vs France)
Temporality: early in an industry, experimentation is rewarded; as it matures, conformity pressure increases

blocks.text: Categories also hierarchize actors (Bourdieu): belonging signals who one is, what one is worth and where one stands.

Middle-status conformity (Phillips & Zuckerman 2001): high-status actors can afford to deviate (secure position), low-status actors have little to lose, middle-status actors conform most – an inverted U of conformity over status.

Durand & Kremp (2016, US orchestras 1879–1969): organizations align with peers to avoid penalties, while conductors conform selectively: low-status Katims programmed for originality, middle-status Ormandy played conventional programmes, high-status Stokowski deviated (Schoenberg).
Central, durable and distinctive attributes answering “who are we as an organization?” (Albert & Whetten 1985).
Audiences penalize offers that do not fit recognized categories (illegitimacy discount).
An actor combining features of typical members of several categories.
Being as different as legitimately possible – balancing differentiation and conformity across dimensions, stakeholders and time.
Middle-status actors conform most; high- and low-status actors deviate more.

sections.heading: Further thinking: using F8 in the exam

blocks.text: For “how does the move relate to the company's identity?” questions: name the central, durable and distinctive attributes from the case, then say whether the move reinforces or contradicts them (and how each audience will react).
When a firm combines categories (app + community, ring + jewellery, wine + tech), discuss the ambiguity paradox and propose a way to orchestrate conformity and distinctiveness.
